text: 📱 New: use the harness from your phone. ruby exe/harness ui --lan lets a phone on your home network chat, start builds, answer the planner and watch progress, while your computer does the work. Read Use it from your phone (LAN mode) first: it is off by default, needs a pairing code, and is for trusted networks only. Off by default. Only on a network you trust. LAN mode opens the app to other devices on your local network. Read the precautions below before you turn it on. Proof-first coding with local models. Models write code; your project's own checks decide whether it survives. VB Harness is an engineering harness that makes local coding agents accountable for their changes. It doesn't try to make the model smarter: it breaks your request into small tasks, has the model write each one in an isolated copy, and keeps a change only when your type check, lint, build and tests pass and an independent review can't prove it wrong. A four-part blog feature, built by a local model on a 6 GB laptop GPU in one unattended run. An animated illustration of a real run (not a screen recording): the plan, code, numbers, review claims and pages come from a real agent-mode run of evaluation task 10, which took 3 hours 28 minutes. The steering note shows the feature and was not part of that run, and the pages are shown in a layout with cover art made for the video; the run's own files are unchanged. Click it for the 1080p, 60 fps video. Get real coding work out of the model on your own machine. The harness plans a feature as small tasks, has your local model implement them one at a time, proves every change with your project's own type check, lint, build and tests, and re-reviews what it built with an evidence gate. It is built around the weak spots of local models: hallucinated APIs and defects, wrong edits, broken JSON, and small context windows. AstroJS is the first supported stack. Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works: LM Studio, Ollama, llama.cpp's server, vLLM, or a hosted API. Documentation: vb-harness.vandbruno.net , with the guides, the cookbook and the design decisions. Status: early development. Everything below works and is tested, but expect rough edges and changes. You don't need to write code: you describe the website in plain words, a model on your own computer builds it, and one click shows it in your browser. Setup takes about 30 minutes, once. If something is missing, the app says what and usually offers a Fix button. Local models make mistakes, so look over the result before you publish it. You need Ruby 3.3+ , git, and a model server; LM Studio or Ollama is the easiest. Then: git clone https://github.com/Viktotovich/vb-harness-for-agentic-building.git cd vb-harness-for-agentic-building ruby exe/harness The app opens in your browser on a start page with three steps: connect a model, add a project, describe what to build. To see a whole build before setting anything up, choose Try the demo there (or run ruby exe/harness demo ): a scripted model builds a tiny sample project, with a failed check, its fix and a review, in under a minute. Then Connect opens Settings → Models , where you choose Use on a model. Switch the text box to Build , pick your project, describe the feature, and choose Start build . If the project is not set up yet (dependencies not installed, a generated folder missing, a package its checks need), the line under the text box says so and offers a Fix button: it shows the exact command, runs it after you confirm, and you build. The one thing it leaves to you is uncommitted changes: commit or stash them. Preview next to the project runs its dev server (for Astro, astro dev ) on 127.0.0.1 and opens it; a finished build has a Preview of what it made. 📱 New: use the harness from your phone. ruby exe/harness ui --lan lets a phone on your home network chat, start builds, answer the planner and watch progress, while your computer does the work. Read Use it from your phone (LAN mode) first: it is off by default, needs a pairing code, and is for trusted networks only. On the command line instead, ruby exe/harness init asks a few questions (Enter accepts each default), and ruby exe/harness run --repo ../my-site --request request.md builds what request.md describes. Stuck? ruby exe/harness doctor --repo ../my-site (or Settings → Check setup ) lists every reason a build would not start, each with what to do, without changing anything or asking a model to write. Your checkout is never changed. The work stays on the harness/<runId> branch until you merge it. git clone https://github.com/Viktotovich/vb-harness-for-agentic-building.git cd vb-harness-for-agentic-building ruby exe/harness --version That is all: there is nothing to install with gem or bundle . To put harness on your PATH, either alias ruby /path/to/vb-harness-for-agentic-building/exe/harness , or build and install the gem locally: gem build vb-harness.gemspec gem install ./vb-harness- * .gem The folder that holds config.json is the harness's home : chats/ , runs/ , logs/ , .cache/ , projects/ and workspaces/ are created next to it. All of them are git-ignored. ruby exe/harness This starts the local app on http://127.0.0.1:4567/ and, on first start, opens your browser on the start page. The sidebar lists your chats, newest first; a chat that started a build shows its state there ( Building , Needs you , Failed , Stopped or ✓), so a waiting build is easy to spot. The model in use and whether it is working sit at the bottom of the sidebar, next to Settings . Connect a model (Settings → Models). The app looks for LM Studio and Ollama on this machine. You can start LM Studio's server, load a downloaded model, or pull an Ollama model, each with one click. For any other server, enter its OpenAI-compatible URL under Another server and, if it needs a key, the name of the environment variable that holds the key (never the key itself). Choose Use on a model: the harness probes it and shows what it found as plain labels, for example "48K context · JSON mode: yes · tools: yes · thinking can be turned off". Plan & review on any model makes it the model the planner, reviewer and verifier use, even on the same server as the first. Settings → How runs work picks the mode (Careful, Balanced or Quick) and the way of working (Pipeline or Agent). Chat. Chat mode is a planning conversation: work out what to build, compare approaches, sketch the steps. Ctrl+Enter (⌘+Enter on macOS) sends; Enter adds a line. Replies stream. When the model thinks first, you see Thinking… 4s with its latest line of thought as it works; afterwards it folds into Thought for 12s above the reply, and a click opens the whole thought process so you can judge how it got there. Chat changes no files. Use as build request under a reply copies it into the text box in Build mode, for you to edit and send: nothing starts until you do. Build. Switch the text box to Build , pick a project (or Add project ), describe the feature, and choose Start build . The line under the text box says what will happen, or what stops the build (uncommitted changes, a project with a problem). A live card in the chat shows the run: If the planner has blocking questions, the card turns amber and asks them in the card itself, one field per question, with Answer and continue . When the run ends, the card shows a short summary, the branch with Copy branch , and View report , which opens the report beside the chat. A stopped or failed run has Resume , which continues where it left off and keeps what was committed. The app only listens on 127.0.0.1 , refuses other host names, and needs a per-start token for every change. Settings → Appearance chooses the look: System (follows your computer's light or dark setting), Dark or Light . Each look has a few colour presets, and you can pick your own colours for the background, cards, text, accent and the three status colours. The app shows the text contrast as you go and warns when it gets hard to read. Only colours change; the font and layout stay the same. The choice is saved in appearance.json next to config.json . Off by default. Only on a network you trust. LAN mode opens the app to other devices on your local network. Read the precautions below before you turn it on. ruby exe/harness ui --lan # your computer's private address, found for you ruby exe/harness ui --lan 192.168.1.20 # or name it The terminal prints an address such as http://192.168.1.20:4567/ and a 6-digit code; the app on the computer shows the same in a banner at the top. Open the address on your phone, type the code, and the phone gets the full app: chat, start builds, answer the planner's questions, send the agent notes, stop and resume, read reports. The app is laid out for phones. What protects it: Precautions: On Windows with WSL: WSL's own address ( 172.x ) cannot be reached from a phone. Turn on WSL's mirrored networking (then use your PC's address), or run the harness on Windows. The harness warns when this looks like the case. ruby exe/harness demo # a whole run on a sample project, no model needed ruby exe/harness init # write config.json, asking a few questions ruby exe/harness doctor --repo /path/to/repo # check everything a run needs, in one list ruby exe/harness run --repo /path/to/repo --request request.md ruby exe/harness status # the newest run: tasks, current step, rejections ruby exe/harness status RUN_ID --watch # refresh every second until it stops ruby exe/harness answer RUN_ID # answer the planner's blocking questions ruby exe/harness steer RUN_ID " a note " # steer a running agent-mode run, or answer its question ruby exe/harness resume RUN_ID # continue after a stop, a crash or new answers ruby exe/harness report RUN_ID # (re)write runs/RUN_ID/report.md and print its path request.md is plain text, as you would write it to a colleague: Add a Badge component at src/components/Badge.astro. It takes a required label and an optional tone, "info" or "warn" (default "info"), and renders < span class = " badge badge--<tone> " >. Use it on the pricing page. Useful options: A plan for --from-plan is the JSON the planner writes ( runs/<id>/plan.json ), and it is checked the same way: { "tasks" : [ { "id" : " T1 " , "title" : " Add the Badge component " , "intent" : " 1-3 sentences: what and why, with every exact value the task needs " , "files" : { "create" : [ " src/components/Badge.astro " ], "modify" : [], "read" : [ " src/styles/global.css " ] }, "dependsOn" : [], "acceptance" : [ { "kind" : " gate " , "gate" : " typecheck " }, { "kind" : " test " , "path" : " tests/badge.test.ts " , "write" : true , "describe" : " what the test asserts " }, { "kind" : " assert " , "text" : " a property the review checks " } ] } ], "questions" : [] } Each task creates or modifies at most maxFilesPerTask files and needs at least one gate or test item; a test path must be a test file. read and modify list existing files or files a task in dependsOn creates. Progress lines go to stderr; the result goes to stdout. Exit codes: 0 done, 1 the run failed (planning failed, a task was blocked, or something regressed), 2 a configuration or environment problem, 3 waiting for your answers. In the app, Build mode works on projects . Add project (next to the project picker under the text box, or on the start page) offers three ways: Clone and New Astro project download code, so the dialog first shows you the exact command and runs it only after you choose Clone project or Create project . The app never lists folders on your disk. Every run works in its own worktree under workspaces/<runId> in the harness's home, on branch harness/<runId> . Folders listed in the stack's dependencyDirs (for Astro, node_modules ) are mirrored into the worktree with hard links, so your project's tools can run there without reinstalling. The harness never writes to them, and every file it writes replaces the link instead of writing through it. To keep the result, merge the branch in your repository: git merge harness/RUN_ID Understanding a run Everything about a run is in runs/<runId>/ : Read this first , at the top of the report when it applies, says what the numbers below do not show: a gate that could not run, review that was off or light, a run that failed or stopped early, a dry run, and anything that changed while the run was paused. Each line says what to do about it. Rejections are the heart of the report: every output the harness threw away is counted by reason, such as "edit search text not found", "typecheck failed", "depends on code not shown" or "needs a value its type forbids". Replies that were discarded and retried with thinking off count too. Rejections show where a model struggles, and they are how you compare models. Findings in the report are only claims confirmed by a failing test. Everything else the review raised is under Questions , clearly marked as unconfirmed. docs/cookbook/astro-landing-page.md builds a small business landing page from an empty folder with a local 16K coder model: the new project, the theme, planning in Chat, the Build request line by line, seven runs (the first two found harness gaps, now fixed; the last four were layout and fixes after reviewing the page), reviewing the branch and merging it. Every stage has a screenshot. Claude Code is good at deciding what to build and at reviewing it; the typing in between is where most of its tokens go. The harness can take that part. Claude writes the request, starts a run, and reads back a short report and a diff, while a model on your own machine does the planning, editing, fixing and reviewing in between. What it saves, measured on the cookbook's third run (eight tasks, a full landing page): About 13 times the model traffic stayed on the local machine. Claude's figures are the sizes of what it would read and write, estimated the way the harness budgets context (three bytes a token, which errs high); they leave out Claude's own system prompt and turns. We have not measured Claude building the same page directly, so this is not a claim about how much that would cost; it would at least read the files, write the 375 lines and check them, with every turn re-sending the conversation. The trade is time. A 16K local model one request at a time took a couple of hours for that page. Hand the harness the work that is clear and self-contained, and keep Claude for the parts that need judgment. How to set it up. Install the harness and connect a local model (see Install and Choosing and checking a model ). Then tell Claude Code how to delegate, in your project's CLAUDE.md : ## Delegating to VB Harness For a self-contained feature (a component, a page, a small refactor), delegate to the local harness instead of writing the code yourself: 1 . Write the request to ` .harness/request.md ` : exact file paths, exact values (colours, sizes, text), what each file imports, and what is out of scope. The harness keeps what the request says and nothing else. 2 . Run it in the background: ` ruby <harness>/exe/harness run --repo . --request .harness/request.md --json ` . 3 . Check on it with ` ruby <harness>/exe/harness status RUN_ID --json ` rather than polling often; runs take minutes to hours. 4 . Exit code 3 means the planner asked questions: answer with ` harness answer RUN_ID --answers answers.json ` . 5 . When it finishes, read ` runs/RUN_ID/report.md ` and ` git diff main...harness/RUN_ID ` . Gates prove the code builds, not that it matches the request, so review it. Merge with ` git merge harness/RUN_ID ` , or send a smaller follow-up request. Any command works the same from Claude's side: --json on every command gives machine-readable output, progress goes to stderr, and the exit code says how the run ended (see Quick start: the command line ). Paste a link to a Figma frame into your request, and the run builds from that design: Add a pricing section to the home page, matching https://www.figma.com/design/FILE/Name?node-id=1-2 In Figma, select the frame and use Copy link . A link to a whole file is refused, because it doesn't say what to build. Create a Figma personal access token with read access to file content, and put it in the FIGMA_TOKEN env var. To use another variable, set "figmaTokenEnv" in config.json . When the run starts, the harness reads each linked frame once and adds it to the run's request.md as a short outline: structure, sizes, spacing, colours, type and wording. Pipeline and agent modes both use it, so the model needs no image support and no Figma tools. A design that can't be read stops the run before any model is called, and the run shows the reason. Limits: the outline is text, so images and icons appear only as named placeholders, and it stops at 5,000 characters, so link a section rather than a whole page. It's read once, so later changes in Figma don't reach a running run. Safety: only links in your request are read, so a model or a repo file can't choose what's fetched. Requests are read-only. The token goes only into the request to Figma, and layer names and text reach models as untrusted data. harness init (or the app's Settings) writes config.json for you. Start from config.example.json ; every value there is a default or a placeholder. Profiles describe model servers; roles say which profile does what: " profiles " : { "default" : { "baseUrl" : " http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1 " , "model" : " auto " , // "auto" uses the first model the server lists "apiKeyEnv" : null , // the NAME of an env var holding a key, or null "contextTokens" : " probe " , // or a number "maxOutputTokens" : 4000 , "thinking" : { "control" : " probe " , "effort" : " low " , "budgetTokens" : null }, "structuredOutput" : " probe " , // json_schema | json_object | prompt "toolCalls" : " probe " , // native | none "continuation" : " probe " , // prefill | continue_final_message | none "timeoutSec" : 900 } }, " roles " : { "planner" : " default " , "implementer" : " default " , "fixer" : " default " , "reviewer" : " default " , "verifier" : " default " , "summarizer" : " default " } Use two profiles to plan and review with a larger model and implement with a faster one. HARNESS_<PROFILE>_BASE_URL and HARNESS_<PROFILE>_MODEL override a profile from the environment. Stacks say how to check a project. The Astro stack in the example (each command runs as npx --offline --no -- <tool> , so a tool that is not installed fails at once and npx never downloads one): Gates are argv arrays, never shell strings. A gate whose tool is missing is reported as skipped , never as passed; it blocks a task only when the task names it in its acceptance. Gates may not install packages, run git or gh , or use npx --yes . Other stack keys: detect (files that identify the stack), alwaysGates , protectedPaths (globs the model may never touch; .git , .husky and node_modules are always protected), dependencyDirs , and docs.local (a local checkout of the framework's docs, used by the review; without it, framework claims abstain instead of being confirmed). Two keys power the app's buttons: setup maps a dependencyDirs folder to the command that creates it, offered as a one-click Fix when it is missing (for example "setup": {"generated": ["npx", "--offline", "--no", "--", "prisma", "generate"]} ; node_modules needs no entry, its fix is the package manager's install with --ignore-scripts ), and preview is the dev server's argv with {port} where the port goes (the example config's Astro stack has ["npx", "--offline", "--no", "--", "astro", "dev", "--host", "127.0.0.1", "--port", "{port}"] ). Two keys carry what a small model gets wrong about the stack, as plain data: fixHints ( {"match": text in a diagnostic, "hint": what to tell the fixer} , shown next to a matching diagnostic) and reviewNotes (facts and pitfalls the reviewer and verifier are given). The example's Astro stack has a few, such as "props are Astro.props " and " {expression} output is escaped"; add your project's own. Limits (defaults): maxFilesPerTask 3, maxFixRounds 3, maxReplanRounds 2, maxDiagnostics 20, maxLookups 6, maxReviewFixTasks 2, wholeFileRewriteMaxBytes 4096, maxGateOutputBytes 204800, maxVerifierCalls 60 (per run), maxRefutedInARow 3. Commits : each task is committed as <type>: <title> in Conventional Commits form, with the type ( feat , fix , chore , docs , test , refactor , style , perf ) chosen by the planner. A plan without a type falls back to T1: <title> . The lines under the subject come from "commit": {"trailer": "..."} , default Gates passed: {gates} . The placeholders are {model} (the implementer's model id), {version} (the harness version), {checks} (how many gates passed) and {gates} (their names), for example "Commit by {model} from vb-harness {version}. {checks} checks passed" . Review ( review , default full ): full reviews every task and the whole run; light skips the per-task review of a small change (80 changed lines or fewer) whose gates passed first time, and keeps the final review; off skips review. In every mode the verifier stops when the run has used maxVerifierCalls , or after maxRefutedInARow claims in a row were refuted by the code; the claims left are recorded as unverified questions, never dropped. Review is the most expensive stage with a small model, so light is a good start. Modes. harness init asks how careful runs should be, and the app's Settings can change it later; either writes the matching settings, which you can still edit by hand: It also asks whether to use one model for everything, or a second model (often a larger one) for the planner, reviewer and verifier, with the implementer and fixer on the first. That writes a planning profile and points those roles at it. In the app, Plan & review on a model does the same, and Settings picks which configured model those roles use. A config the app creates starts Balanced, like one from init . Agent mode ( "mode": "agent" , or --mode agent ) trades speed for accuracy. Instead of one structured reply per step, each task is worked by an agent with tools: it reads, lists and searches the code, edits files (exact search-and-replace, whole files, and long new files in parts), and runs the project's gates and the commands you allow, until it calls finish . Its finish is a claim, not a result: the harness then runs the task's gates itself, and sends any failure back to the same agent, which keeps what it already read, until the gates pass or agent.maxRounds runs out. Before planning, an investigating agent reads the repository (it cannot change files) and its findings go to the planner, so plans and bug fixes start from the code as it is. Tasks may change up to agent.maxFilesPerTask files. The safety rules do not change. Writes stay in the worktree and outside protectedPaths ; tool output is fenced as untrusted; only gates mark a task done. The agent runs only the stack's gates and the commands you declare under agent.commands , by name: an argument written exactly as {name} is filled from a declared parameter, either path (an existing file in the repository) or word (letters, digits and . _ : / @ - , never starting with - , and never an absolute path, drive letter or .. ). The model never writes a command line. Check configuration ( package.json , tsconfig*.json , *.config.* , linter configs and the like) and tests that already exist can be changed only when the plan names them, so an agent cannot make a gate pass by weakening it. Acceptance tests. An implementer's own tests share its misunderstandings. With agent.acceptanceTests on, the test a task's plan asks for is written first, from the request, by a separate agent on roles.tester (the reviewer's model unless you set it). The implementer can read that test but not change it. Halfway through agent.maxRounds , a test the code still fails gets one look from its author, who may correct it only against the request. Work that passes such a test counts as done even if the agent never called finish . A task with no test in its plan, or a stack with no test gate, works as before. When an agent stops early. An agent that runs out of steps, or stops without calling finish , gets a limited number of further tries, and each one changes something. First a new conversation, told by the harness what is already in the repository. Then a smaller job: the harness runs the checks and gives the agent only what is left, with half the steps. Then, if roles.rescuer names a different profile from roles.implementer , that model takes over. After that the task blocks, and the report says what was tried. Steering a running agent. While an agent-mode run works, harness steer RUN_ID "use the existing Button component" (or the note box on its card in the app) sends it a note, which the agent reads before its next step, as your words. An agent can also ask you a question with ask_user when the task is ambiguous: the question shows on the card, in the events and in run.json , and your next note is the answer. If none comes within agent.askTimeoutSec , the agent decides for itself and says in its summary what it assumed. In the app, Settings switches the way of working between Pipeline and Agent, and an agent-mode card's Agent activity lists each agent's steps. Agent mode makes many more model calls than the pipeline; with a local model, expect a task to take several times longer. Models without native tool calls use a JSON reply protocol, one tool per reply. A red baseline. When a blocking gate already fails before the run, intake says so (an event, and a line at the top of the report); tasks are still judged only on new problems. Set requireGreenBaseline to true to stop the run there instead, before any model call (exit code 2). A dry run ( harness run --dry-run , or "dryRun": true for every run on the command line) shows what a run would start from without calling a model: the stack, each gate's baseline result, the plan's problems when a plan is given (all but the context-size check, which needs the model), and what would happen next. It exits 0 when nothing found would stop a real run, 1 for plan problems, 2 for a failing baseline under requireGreenBaseline . The app's Build is never a dry run. gateEnvAllow lists extra environment variables your gates need; everything that looks like a secret is removed from the gates' environment otherwise. Nothing about specific models is built in. On first use, the harness probes each model: its context size, whether it can return JSON or call tools, whether its thinking can be turned off, whether it can continue a reply it started, and how fast it is. Values you set in a profile override the probe. Results are cached in .cache/probe/ . Practical advice: The harness assumes the model can be wrong or manipulated, and limits what it can do: Each of these has a test in test/guardrails_test.rb . See SECURITY.md to report a vulnerability. eval/ holds ten Astro tasks of increasing size (a component, a utility, pages, a content collection, API routes, an island, i18n routes, a blog) with hidden acceptance tests the harness never sees while it works. ruby eval/run_eval.rb --config config.json --profile-map eval/profile-map.example.json It prints one table per profile mapping: solved, solved without fix rounds, regressions, findings confirmed, fix rounds, tokens and time, plus tokens and time per role. Preparing the starting repository is described in eval/README.md . Chart redrawn from the data in Martin Alderson's Which programming languages are most token-efficient? (values read off the published chart). The study counted tokens for the same Rosetta Code tasks in each language using a GPT-4 tokenizer. Its author calls it an illustrative comparison, not a rigorous study. TypeScript was left out for lack of tasks. ruby bin/check # syntax and warnings, guardrail scans, all tests ruby bin/test # tests only (or: ruby bin/test test/path_test.rb) Tests need no model server, network or GPU. There is no hosted CI: run bin/check before opening a pull request and paste its summary, as described in CONTRIBUTING.md . Design decisions are recorded in docs/decisions.md ; a manual checklist for the app is in docs/ui-checklist.md . Apache-2.0, by V and Bruno LLC . See LICENSE and NOTICE .
